name: Pinchbeck Brown
lede: Pinchbeck brown is a brown named for a metal, listed in early nineteenth-century color nomenclatures.

sections.title: A metal's brown
sections.body:
The name appears in Baty's survey of historic color nomenclatures [1]. In Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's scheme, which lists 110 colors, *Pinchbeck-brown* sits between yellowish-brown and wood-brown, glossed in brackets as tombac [1]. The earlier 1814 version, with 108 colors, lists that slot as Tombac-brown [1]. Syme's lists tie each color to examples from minerals, animals and plants [1].

Werner's scheme began as a way to identify minerals, and Syme added animal and plant examples [1]. Pinchbeck brown stood among the browns beside hair-brown, clove-brown and liver-brown, and the list was meant to be checked against painted swatches [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a very common tone in painting. In our archive of museum paintings, a color near this swatch is present in 1,528 works, 6.43 per cent of the archive [2]. The earliest is a work of about 1200 and the latest dates from 1934 [2]. Among painters, John Singer Sargent has 15 works with it [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [2].

questions.q: What bracketed alternative name does Baty's list give for pinchbeck-brown?
True or false: the name refers to a metal-like golden brown.

openers: Pinchbeck brown was a color in an 1821 nomenclature for naturalists, glossed as tombac.

issues: 1814 list has Tombac-brown, not Pinchbeck-brown: fixed false 'already has it'. Removed unsupported 'no everyday use today' and 'golden' in lede; naturalist scope corrected to minerals plus animal/plant examples.
